catalog_quote: Syllables with long vowels (indicated in the data with a double vowel) and diphthongs are considered to be heavy and always attract stress (except in word final position). ... Stress in Asheninca follows a left-to-right iambic pattern – where feet can be (LL), (LH), or (H) – as illustrated by the fact that stress falls on all heavy syllables (as in 32b) and on even-numbered syllables in a string of light syllables (32a). Final syllables are considered to be extrametrical and are never stressed, even if the final syllable is heavy (e.g., [jíñaa] ‘water’, *[jiñáa]). sweep_summary: Two sweep items. (1) Pater 2000 (Phonology) is about English secondary stress; Glottolog's own record shows it was attached to pich1237 by a 'computerized assignment from "ranked"', and the Cambridge abstract names no language but English: irrelevant, priority none. The real gain: the English original, Payne 1990 'Asheninca stress patterns' (the catalog's unheld primary; DOI paywalled, archive.org scan lending-restricted), was read first-hand at snippet level through the Internet Archive full-text-search highlight API with an identifier filter, yielding 194 verbatim scanned fragments (saved). They give the core statements directly: alternating stress from the second syllable, final syllable never stressed (extrametrical) except three lexically stressed suffixes, Heavy (branching-nucleus) syllables always stressed unless word-final, primary stress on the rightmost stressed syllable unless a heavier syllable outranks it, four-grade weight scale Heavy/Normal/Light/Extra-light, rapid-speech deletions, and fn.1 fixing the variety as Pichis. This confirms the catalog's weight-hedged coding and supersedes the second-hand McGarrity 2003/Rasin 2017 quotations as the deciding quote, though only as fragments; the full chapter (or the 1991 Spanish version) is still worth acquiring (high) for the complete rule (32) conditions and example sets. The held J. Payne 1989 Lecciones pp.34-43 was re-read and matches the 1990 fragments point for point. All fetched sources

new_statements.reading: Pichis Ashéninka has weight-sensitive, left-to-right alternating (iambic) stress: stress starts on the second syllable and hits every second syllable, the final syllable is extrametrical and never stressed (save three lexically stressed word-final suffixes), Heavy syllables (branching nucleus: long vowel or diphthong) are always stressed unless word-final and restart the count, and primary stress goes to the rightmost stressed syllable unless a heavier syllable in the relevant window outranks it (nucleus a counts as heavier than e/o/i; a Normal penult beats a stressed Light final). Syllable weight is a four-grade scale Heavy > Normal > Light (Ci) > Extra-light (tsi/shi-type, which reject stress), with rapid-speech deletion of Light-syllable stresses. This is exactly the system the catalog codes as weight-hedged with CVV heavy, final extrametrical and right-edge primary; it confirms the coding and adds the four-grade scale, the nucleus-quality tie-break and the three-suffix exception.

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both the deciding quote (McGarrity 2003 pp.178-179, fn.17) and the dq quote (Rasin 2017 sec.5.3 pp.28-29) are verbatim in the held text files at the stated locators. (2) The classification rests on second-hand renderings (2003 dissertation, 2017 ms) of J. Payne 1990, the dedicated primary stress study, which we do not hold and could not fetch (paywall; De Gruyter refused scripted fetch). (3) But the record overlooks a held primary source by the same author on the same variety: J. Payne 1989 Lecciones (SLP 28, Pichis) pp.34-43, whose Spanish rules match the coding point for point (alternating stress from the 2nd syllable on even syllables, never the final; VV/diphthong syllables always stressed except word-finally, even when adjacent; Ci weak, tsi/shi 'dead'; primary stress on the last heavy within the final four-syllable window

sources.quote: p.36: "En las palabras formadas por sílabas normales, el patrón de acentuación empieza en la segunda sílaba y se acentúan todas las sílabas pares a la derecha, pero no la última sílaba de la palabra"; p.37: "Todas las sílabas fuertes son acentuadas, salvo cuando están al final de la palabra, sin importar el patrón de acentuación de la palabra. Son acentuadas aun cuando estén seguidas en la palabra."; p.42: "El acento primario recae sobre la última sílaba fuerte que puede ser la penúltima, la antepenúltima y la antes de la antepenúltima sílaba. Después del acento primario, no hay acento secundario ... Si ninguna de las cuatro últimas sílabas es fuerte, el acento primario recae en la última sílaba que lleva acento." [EN: In words of normal syllables the stress pattern starts on the second syllable and every even syllable to the right is stressed, but not the last syllable of the word; all strong (VV/diphthong) syllables are stressed except word-finally, regardless of the pattern, even when adjacent; primary stress falls on the last strong syllable, which may be the penult, antepenult or pre-antepenult; after the primary stress there is no secondary; if none of the last four syllable…
sources.note: Same author, same Pichis variety, same system stated pedagogically in Spanish: four syllable strengths fuerte/normal/débil/muerta = Payne 1990's Heavy/Normal/Light/Extra-light; alternating stress from the 2nd syllable, never the final; strong syllables always stressed unless final; primary stress on the last strong syllable within the final four, else the rightmost stress (p.43 exception: if the last stressed syllable is weak Ci and the preceding stressed one is normal, the normal one takes primary). Matches the 1990 snippets point for point.
